title: Pick the locator that survives a redesign
prompt:
Splitwise-lite's expense list renders like this: ```html
  • Dinner: $45.50
  • Taxi: $18.00
  • Museum: $24.00
``` Next sprint, a designer will switch the list to a card grid, change every class, and sort expenses by date instead of insertion order. Which locator for **the Remove button of the Taxi expense** is most likely to keep working, and to fail only if users really couldn't remove the taxi?
hints: Rule out anything that depends on classes, DOM nesting or position: all three are about to change.
Prefer what a user perceives: the button's role and name, scoped to the row that mentions Taxi.
explanation: `page.getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Taxi' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Remove' })` describes the target the way a person would: the Remove button in the taxi row. It doesn't care about classes, nesting or order, so the redesign leaves it intact, and it fails if the row stops being a list item with an accessible Remove button, which is a real regression for keyboard and screen reader users. If the redesign uses cards that aren't list items any more, the test fails loudly and points at a genuine accessibility change, which is worth a conversation. The CSS path and `nth(1)` break on the first class change or re-sort; the test id survives restyling but proves nothing about what users can see or reach, and only one row has it.

css-path.why: It encodes classes, nesting and position, all of which the redesign changes, so it breaks even though removing the taxi still works.

nth.why: It relies on the taxi being second. After sorting by date it would silently click a different expense's Remove button, which is worse than failing.

role-filter.why: Correct. It finds the button by role and name inside the row that mentions Taxi, so classes, layout and order can change freely.

text-only.why: It matches three buttons, so any action on it fails with a strict mode violation, and it says nothing about which expense you meant.

test-id.why: It survives restyling, but test ids are invisible to users and the last resort: the button could lose its label or be hidden from assistive tech and this would still pass.
